Collector first. Seller second. This is the buying guide we'd want ourselves before putting money into the 30th anniversary set, written from Victoria, Australia.

What the 30th Celebration set is

Pokémon 30th Celebration is the Japanese anniversary expansion in the current Mega Evolution series, set code M6a. It released in Japan in September 2026 and it is the box every Australian collector has been asking us about since. As an "a" set it sits alongside Storm Emeralda (M6) rather than replacing it, which is why you'll see both on our shelf at the same time.

We won't list chase cards here. Pull rates and card lists shift as the set is opened, so rely on the printed set list in the box and the set code on every pack rather than a blog post that will age.

Pack and box counts

  • 20 packs per box, which is fewer than the usual 30 for a Japanese main set.
  • 6 cards per pack, which is one more than the usual 5.
  • Every pack carries the M6a set code. If a pack in your box doesn't, stop and send us a photo.

"No outer shrink" explained

Our M6a box is listed as No Outer Shrink. That means the printed Pokémon Card Game outer film has been removed before export, but the box seals and every one of the 20 packs are untouched and factory sealed. Japanese distributors do this with some allocations and it is normal for this set. It is not a resealed box. What you check on a no-shrink box is the packs: crisp, even crimps, the same set code on each, no glossy or off-colour packs. The spot-a-fake guide covers the tests in detail.

Why buy the Japanese box

Japanese Pokémon product is printed by the same company that prints the English set, with tighter quality control, better card stock and holofoil, and it reaches shelves months ahead of the English equivalent. For an anniversary set there is also the simple fact that this is the version Japan celebrated with. If you're new to the difference, read Japanese vs English Pokémon cards first and then our 2026 guide to Japanese booster boxes in Australia.

How HOKO imports it

Every M6a box we sell is imported from Japan by HOKO, direct from our Japanese distributor. Import freight from Japan is included in the price. Boxes are checked in hand in Victoria and dispatched tracked from Victoria within 2–4 business days once it lands. Postage within Australia on sealed is a flat tracked rate, free on orders of $250 or more. For Christmas, order Japanese sealed by Monday 7 December 2026.

Authenticity is guaranteed. If a sealed item we sell isn't genuine, you get a full refund. Returns are accepted within 7 days of delivery if the item is not as described. Sealed and international orders are final sale, and none of this limits your rights under the Australian Consumer Law.

Where to buy

  • Pokémon 30th Celebration (M6a) Japanese Booster Box — No Outer Shrink
  • Every Japanese sealed box we have right now, newest releases first

Collecting One Piece as well? Our Heroines Edition vol.2 (EB-05) pre-order guide covers the next Japanese box landing after this one.

Questions about a box you've already got? Send us a photo before you open it and we'll sort it. We sell on eBay too, with 1.5K sold and 100% positive feedback, and the same boxes are on hokocollectables.com.

Collector first. Seller second. Here's what we know about the second Heroines extra booster, what to expect from a box, and how pre-ordering the Japanese version works from Victoria, Australia.

What EB-05 is

Extra Booster ONE PIECE Heroines Edition vol.2, set code EB-05, is Bandai's follow-up to the first Heroines Edition (EB-03). Like its predecessor it is built around the women of One Piece, with new art across leaders, characters and events. It is an extra booster, so it sits beside the main OP sets rather than replacing them, and the card pool is smaller and more focused than a numbered booster.

Release date

Bandai's Japanese product page lists Saturday 31 October 2026. The English edition follows a day earlier in Western time zones, which is why some Australian retailers show 30 October. The Japanese release-event period at Bandai's authorised shops runs from release day through to mid-November.

What's in a box

  • 6 cards per pack (extra boosters run smaller packs than the 12-card main sets).
  • 24 packs per box.
  • 75 cards in the regular set plus 2 DON!! cards: 7 leaders, 29 commons, 21 rares, 9 super rares, 1 secret rare and 8 special cards, per Bandai's card list.

We'll leave pull rates alone until boxes are being opened. Judge the set on the printed list, not on hype.

Japanese vs English for this set

Japanese One Piece product ships first, uses Bandai's Japanese print run, and for Heroines sets the Japanese alt-art versions are the ones most collectors chase. If you want the broad comparison, our 2026 guide to Japanese Pokémon and One Piece booster boxes covers it, and the spot-a-fake guide applies to Bandai boxes too: printed outer shrink with Bandai logos, one clean heat seal, matching set codes on every pack.

If you collect Pokémon or One Piece in Australia, you've probably noticed Japanese booster boxes turning up more and more. Some people swear by them. Others aren't sure what they're actually getting. This is the plain version: how Japanese sealed differs from English, what it really costs to get a box into Australia, which sets I've got right now and how delivery works.

Japanese vs English sealed: what's actually different

The box itself

A Japanese box is not a Japanese-language copy of an English box. The product is built differently.

  • Pokémon. A standard Japanese expansion box is 30 packs of 5 cards. An English booster box is 36 packs of 10. Japanese "high class" sets, such as Terastal Festival ex, come as 10 packs of 10 cards instead.
  • One Piece. Japanese and English boxes both hold 24 packs, but a Japanese pack has 6 cards and an English pack has 12.

Fewer cards per box is the main reason a Japanese box costs less than its English equivalent. It's a smaller product, so compare them per box, not per pack.

Print quality

Japanese cards have a long-standing reputation among collectors for cleaner centring, fewer print lines and a slightly different finish on the holos. In my experience that reputation is mostly earned. But I won't promise any individual card is perfect, because factory variation exists in every language. If centring matters to you, it matters in both languages.

The card stock and backs are different too. Japanese Pokémon cards have a different back from English cards. That's worth knowing if you ever plan to mix them in a binder or a sleeve set.

Pull rates

Here's the honest answer: neither The Pokémon Company nor Bandai publishes pull rates for Japanese product. Anyone quoting you exact odds is guessing or working from a small sample. Collectors widely report that Japanese boxes feel more consistent from box to box. I'm not going to put numbers on it that I can't back up.

Release timing and exclusives

Japanese sets usually release months ahead of the English version. Some sets and special boxes are only ever printed in Japanese. The English sets often combine Japanese releases, so the set names and codes don't line up one to one. That's why every box in the store carries its Japanese set code (M6, sv8a, OP-17 and so on). You can check exactly which release you're buying.

Playing vs collecting

Japanese cards have Japanese text. Most Australian buyers open them for the pulls and the art, or keep the box sealed. If you want cards for local tournaments, check your event's rules on Japanese-language cards before you buy.

What it costs to land a box in Australia

The yen price you see on a Japanese retailer's site is only the start. By the time a box reaches your door in Australia, these costs are in it:

  • The box. The yen price in Japan.
  • The exchange rate. Yen to Australian dollars on the day the order is paid.
  • Freight. A full booster box is a proper parcel, not a letter. International tracked freight from Japan is a real part of the price, especially for a single box.
  • Insurance. A sealed box is worth insuring on the way over.
  • Selling costs. Card processing and platform fees on the sale.

The import freight from Japan is already in every HOKO box price, in Australian dollars. The only thing added at checkout is the local leg: a flat $15.25 Australia Post tracked parcel from Victoria to your door.

GST and the A$1,000 line

Australia treats imported goods differently either side of A$1,000 per consignment.

  • A$1,000 or less. The parcel clears without a customs bill to the buyer at the door. One box sits well under that line.
  • Over A$1,000 in a single consignment. The parcel goes through formal import clearance, and GST, any applicable duty and an import processing charge are assessed before it's released.

So if you're planning a multi-box order, the total can cross that line. Message me before you order and we'll talk through how it ships.

What's in stock right now

Everything below is a factory-sealed Japanese booster box, listed with its set code. Stock moves fast, so the Japanese Sealed collection is always the current list. Boxes currently run from $115 to $470.

  • Nihil Zero (M3): no outer shrink

  • Mega Brave (M1L)

A note on the "no outer shrink" boxes. Japanese Pokémon boxes normally come in an outer shrink wrap. These don't, and the listing says so up front. The packs inside are factory sealed. If an outer wrap matters to you, pick one of the others.

One Piece

  • OP-16
  • OP-12
  • OP-11
  • OP-07

After a set that isn't listed? Message me. New boxes are added as each batch is confirmed.

What to buy in 2026

I'm not going to tell you a box is an investment. Nobody knows that, and sealed product goes down as well as up. What I can tell you is how I'd think about it.

  • Opening for the pulls: start with the newest sets. That's where the chase cards people are actually looking for are, and where the singles market is most active.
  • Keeping it sealed: older sets that are already out of print in Japan are the ones that get harder to find. Buy what you'd be happy to own either way.
  • Trying Japanese for the first time: a standard Pokémon expansion or a main One Piece set is the easiest place to start. Save the premium and extra boxes for once you know you like the format.
  • Checking value before you buy: look at recent eBay sold listings for the chase cards from that set, not asking prices. Anyone can list a card for anything.

Japanese or English of the same set?

If a set exists in both languages, ask yourself what you want at the end. If you want to grade the hits or keep a clean binder, Japanese is a good place to start. If you want to play at an English-language event, or you'd rather read the cards, buy English. And if you're chasing one specific card, it's usually cheaper to buy that single than to open boxes hoping for it, in either language. Opening is for the fun of opening.

How delivery works

These boxes are imported from Japan by HOKO in small batches. Here's what happens after you order:

  1. Your order comes through to me and I match it to the next batch from our partner in Japan.
  2. The box lands with me in Victoria and I send it on by tracked parcel.
  3. You get an email with the tracking number as soon as it's sent, and you can follow it the whole way.

Dispatched tracked from Victoria within 2–4 business days. If something looks slow, message me and I'll chase it.

Every Japanese box also has a returns note on its product page. Read it before you buy, because sealed product is treated differently from singles.

Why buy from HOKO

HOKO is one person, not a warehouse. I've been collecting for 20 years and selling since 2023, from Victoria, Australia. Every listing names the exact set and set code, says plainly when a box has no outer shrink, and doesn't dress anything up. If something isn't right, you're talking to the person who listed it.

Browse the Japanese Sealed collection →

Collector first. Seller second.
— Ethan
